title: Governed Deduction: Policy-Grounded Premise Authorization Beyond Relevance
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 25 Sep 2026]
    Title:Governed Deduction: Policy-Grounded Premise Authorization Beyond Relevance
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Reasoning systems usually treat premise use as a question of relevance: if a fact is available and useful, it may be selected for inference. Authorization imposes a different constraint: a premise may be represented and logically usable but not permitted for a particular local transition. We formalize this distinction as Governed Deduction (GD), with a transition-local admission predicate admit(p, tau, S). From an independently produced RBAC-augmented Spider benchmark, we construct 4,461 matched authorization pairs in which the same query premise and policy state support permitted and denied consuming transitions. An initial joint controller reaches 99.19% held-out accuracy, but a transition-only control reaches 100%, exposing a role-name shortcut. After a frozen, label-independent context-local role permutation removes that shortcut, premise/state-only, transition-only, and joint linear controllers all score exactly 50% on 1,856 held-out edges, while a symbolic policy oracle remains at 100%. The result is a controlled negative finding: the benchmark instantiates policy-grounded authorization beyond relevance, but the frozen linear representation does not recover the relation. Matched one-sided controls and leakage audits are therefore essential for evaluating learned policy-sensitive reasoning.

report.summary: A new paper argues AI reasoning must separate 'is this fact relevant?' from 'is this fact permitted?', and finds standard learned models fail the policy-authorization task, scoring at chance.
report.background: Most reasoning and retrieval systems, including retrieval-augmented generation and agentic tool use, decide which facts to use by relevance: if a fact is available and useful, it gets selected. That assumption breaks down in governed settings such as enterprise data, healthcare, finance, and multi-tenant AI agents, where access-control rules (RBAC/ABAC) say a fact may be visible and logically usable yet still forbidden for a specific inference step. Building on the Spider text-to-SQL benchmark, the authors create RBAC-augmented data with matched permitted/denied pairs, isolating authorization from relevance. Their finding matters because policy compliance is becoming a core requirement for deployed AI systems, and it cannot be assumed to emerge from better relevance ranking or larger language models alone.
key_points: The paper formalizes 'Governed Deduction', adding a transition-local predicate admit(p, tau, S) that asks whether premise p is allowed in a specific inference step given policy state S. This separates authorization from relevance — a fact can be available and useful but still off-limits locally.

The authors build 4,461 matched authorization pairs from an RBAC-augmented Spider benchmark, where identical query premises and policy states support both permitted and denied transitions. Matching removes many easy shortcuts and forces models to use actual policy semantics.

An initial joint controller hit 99.19% held-out accuracy, but a transition-only control reached 100%, revealing a role-name shortcut: the model was reading the role label rather than reasoning about policy.

After a frozen, label-independent context-local role permutation removed that shortcut, premise-only, transition-only, and joint linear controllers all scored exactly 50% on 1,856 held-out edges, while a symbolic policy oracle stayed at 100%.

The paper frames this as a deliberate negative result: the benchmark does test authorization beyond relevance, but a frozen linear representation cannot recover it, so matched one-sided controls and leakage audits are essential when evaluating learned policy-sensitive reasoning.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a caution against treating compliance as a side effect of scale or better retrieval. Teams shipping agents that touch private data need explicit policy engines and audits, not just relevance-ranked context. For developers, the practical lesson is methodological: single-sided benchmarks and role labels create leakage that inflates accuracy, so evaluation should include matched permitted/denied pairs, one-sided controls, and label-independent permutations. For regular users, it means a model that answers fluently may still be using information it should not, and vice versa — silently withholding legitimate facts. Policy-grounded reasoning looks like a distinct capability requiring symbolic or hybrid designs rather than an emergent property of current architectures.
report.tools: To follow up, read the paper's benchmark construction alongside the original Spider text-to-SQL dataset. For implementing policy checks, look at Open Policy Agent (Rego), AWS Cedar, and Google Zanzibar-style authorization models. For hybrid reasoning, symbolic solvers such as Z3, Datalog engines like Soufflé, and Prolog remain useful oracles. Guardrail frameworks including NeMo Guardrails and LangChain callbacks can host admission checks, and arXiv's own Connected Papers, alphaXiv, and Hugging Face links help track follow-up work and released code.
